on the second morning, i repeated the main steps with voiceover on the iphone. the room details were easier to follow when swiping down the page than when using the rotor's links list, because the repeated “More” names appeared together there too. the room filters could be reached and changed, and voiceover announced whether each was selected. after changing a filter, the results updated without a page reload. the number of matching rooms changed visually, but the new count was not announced automatically. i could still reach the updated list by continuing to swipe, so the results were present; the missing announcement was most noticeable when the list became shorter and the next room moved upward on the screen.

the request form had fields for name, email, group size, and a short note about equipment needs. the labels were announced when i moved into the fields, and the required fields were identified. the email field used an appropriate input type on the phone, which brought up the email keyboard. i deliberately left the name field empty and activated the request button. the page displayed a message saying the name was required, but it was not announced by voiceover until i navigated back to the top of the form. the same message was available to nvda after i moved through the form again. the field itself did not receive a visible error outline on the phone, although the text message was shown above it.

She said the west loop had a few older pedestals and that the maintenance crew had replaced two covers in the spring. The subtitle file for the Harbor Room concert arrived at 8:12 on Thursday evening, less than a day before the doors were due to open. It was named `harbor_final_v7.srt`, although the production folder also contained files called `harbor_final_v7b` and `harbor_final_revised_USE_THIS`. Mara, the venue’s access coordinator, copied the newest export into a separate working folder and wrote the arrival time on the paper checklist. The band had played the room twice before, but this was the first show for which the venue had arranged live captions on the side screens as well as a downloadable subtitle file for the recording.

The recording was a little under ninety minutes long. It included the opening announcement, the full set, and a short conversation between the singer, Lena Ortiz, and the audience near the end. The subtitle file contained 684 cues, with timecodes based on the camera feed rather than the soundboard recording. That difference mattered: the camera audio was about four tenths of a second behind the mix, and the delay changed slightly after the interval. Mara noted both offsets before she started comparing the text with the recording. She did not want the team to mistake a timing issue for a missing line.

1. The first pass

Mara listened from the opening announcement while following each cue on her laptop. The first minute was straightforward. The house manager said, “Welcome to the Harbor Room. Please keep the center aisle clear,” and the caption appeared on both screens before the audience began to applaud. A few cues had been split at natural pauses, which made them easier to read from the back of the room. In one place, however, the file displayed “doors close at half past eight” while the announcement clearly said “doors open at half past eight.” Mara marked the cue for correction and replayed that section twice before moving on.

The band’s first song was called “Paper Satellites,” not “Paper Satellite,” as it appeared in the set list attached to the email. The lyrics were not supplied in advance, so Mara checked the audio rather than trying to fill in uncertain words from the band’s website. Most of the lines were clear, but the mix buried a brief phrase under a cymbal crash. She left the existing wording in place and added a comment for the caption operator to listen again during sound check. In a subtitle file, a confident-looking guess could be harder to notice than an obvious blank, especially when the audience had no other way to check the line.

At 9:03, the caption operator, Dev, called from the control booth. He had noticed that the live display and the recording export disagreed about the song break. The live system showed a short silence after cue 214, while the file ran the singer’s introduction directly into the next song. Mara checked the camera recording and found that the export had trimmed seven seconds of crowd noise. The singer’s introduction was still present, but its first sentence began earlier than the audio actually did. She adjusted the cue boundary to match the recording and sent Dev the new timecode, keeping the longer pause on the live screen so the audience would not see text during the applause.

2. Names, timing, and audience notes

The second pass focused on names and on-screen information. Lena introduced the violinist as “Nico Vale,” while the tour sheet spelled his surname Vail. Dev asked whether the subtitle should follow the spoken introduction or the tour sheet. Mara sent a short message to the band manager, who confirmed that the correct spelling was Vale. The manager also confirmed the name of the guest drummer, Simone Park, whose surname had been omitted from the first export. Mara corrected both names and checked that the changes appeared in the cue list, the plain-text transcript, and the version prepared for the recording.

A separate note from the venue asked that the file identify the two songs performed in the encore. The recording showed the band returning after the lights came up, but the camera did not capture the printed set list. Mara checked the announcement made by the stage manager, then compared it with the titles spoken by Lena before each song. The first was “North Window”; the second was “Small Hours.” She added the titles as brief on-screen cues, not as lyrics, and made sure the cue for “Small Hours” did not cover the interpreter’s hands in the lower corner of the wide shot.

The subtitle file also included audience speech near the front row. A person asked whether the venue would run a late bus after the show, and Lena replied that the box office had a printed schedule. Mara kept the question and answer because they were audible and relevant to the conversation, but she did not add a route number: nobody said one. The venue’s travel page listed two different departure times, and the production team had not asked her to verify them. In her notes, she wrote that the box office schedule should remain visible on the lobby noticeboard until the final audience members had left.

In the final section, Lena thanked the volunteer team and said the Harbor Room had kept a jar of earplugs by the entrance for years. The caption in the file read “a jar of earplugs by the interest,” an error caused by a noisy consonant in the room recording. Mara listened to the isolated channel, checked the same sentence in the live-captions log, and confirmed “entrance.” She repaired the word and then reviewed the whole sentence in context. The brief laugh afterward belonged to the audience, not to Lena, so Mara did not attach it to the spoken line or turn it into a speaker label.

By 10:26, the revised file had passed the timing check on both the camera recording and the soundboard mix. Mara saved it as `harbor_room_concert_access.srt` and moved the earlier exports into an archive folder without deleting them. Dev loaded the new version onto the side-screen system and checked the opening announcement, the two encore titles, and the last spoken cue. Before leaving, Mara wrote the remaining sound-check note beside the cymbal-masked lyric and handed the paper checklist to the morning technician. The venue’s recording team would receive the subtitle file with the corrected names and timecodes, while the unresolved lyric stayed marked for a final listen at the next sound check.

We installed the new audio guide at the north entrance on a Monday in April, after the old handsets began losing their charge before lunchtime. The museum kept the galleries open during the change, and visitors could still borrow a paper map while the staff tested the devices at the desk. Each handset has a small screen, a speaker, and one raised button for starting or pausing a track. The volume controls sit on the side, and the numbered track list appears after the welcome message. We planned the trial for six weeks so the team could hear how people used the guide during both quiet mornings and crowded afternoons.

The actual cost of the replacement headset was 70.21, not 153.48. The higher amount belonged to a different equipment order from the previous year and was not the price paid for these headsets. We bought twelve replacement headsets from the supplier, and the invoice lists the unit price and shipping separately. The total for this purchase was recorded in the museum equipment ledger, and the visitor services manager checked it against the receipt before the invoice was filed. The old headsets had cracked ear cups, but their cords and plugs were still usable, so the technician kept several as spare parts rather than putting them back into circulation.

We set the charging cabinet beside the information desk because staff can see its indicator lights from the entrance. The cabinet holds sixteen handsets and has a printed slot number inside each space. At closing time, the attendant checks the slots and puts any device with less than half a charge into the overnight row. The next morning, the guide lead confirms the screen brightness and plays the first track on two handsets before the doors open. This routine takes about eight minutes when every device has been returned, and longer if a visitor has taken a handset into the courtyard by mistake.

Section One: Room Sequence. The opening track explains the building was a railway office before it became a museum and points out the original iron columns near the ticket desk. Track two introduces the map gallery and asks listeners to look for the blue line painted along the floor. Track three describes the glass cases without asking visitors to touch them, and track four is a short account of the river settlement shown in the west room. The guide does not require visitors to follow the tracks in order, and the screen lets them return to the list at any time. The access note on the first page says that a printed transcript is available from the desk.

We recorded the main narration in a small meeting room upstairs with the door closed and the ventilation fan switched off. The voice artist read each passage at a steady pace and left a pause after the names of people and places so listeners could look at the relevant label. The museum educator listened to the full recording and asked us to correct the pronunciation of two family names before the files were sent to the technician. She also noticed that the east gallery track described a portrait as being on the left when it is on the right. The technician changed that direction and kept the rest of the narration unchanged.

When we tested the guide with visitors, one person said, “The room is quieter when the narration leaves a little space between the sentences.” That comment led us to check the pause lengths with the speaker held at normal listening volume. The sound was clear beside the display cases, but the first version was difficult to hear next to the large street-facing window. We moved the group listening point three steps farther into the room and added a note on the screen suggesting that visitors lower the volume before using the guide near other people. We did not add background music because the gallery already has a low, steady sound from its climate equipment.

The visitor services team also reviewed the instructions printed on the back of each handset. The original card told people to press the raised button once to begin and once again to stop the track. Staff found that some visitors expected a second press to restart the audio, so we changed the wording to explain that a second press pauses playback and the same button starts it again. The team kept the instruction short enough to fit beside the return reminder and added a small drawing of the button. The cards are wiped each evening and replaced when the corners curl or the ink begins to fade.

We keep a daily note of how many guides leave the desk and how many come back before closing. The figures are not used to identify individual visitors, and the sheet has no space for names. On the first Friday, the desk lent out thirty-eight handsets and received thirty-seven before the galleries closed. The missing device was found the next morning on a bench near the education room and had not been damaged. The attendant entered the return time in the maintenance log and placed it in the cabinet after checking its battery. That record helped the team distinguish a late return from a device that needed repair.

The audio guide is available in English during the trial, and visitors can ask the desk for a transcript if listening is not convenient. The staff have a second set of instructions for school groups because teachers sometimes collect several handsets together and return them in one batch. The group instructions ask the teacher to count the devices before leaving the desk and again at the end of the visit. No deposit is required, and the staff do not reserve handsets in advance. On busy days, the desk may ask a group to wait while returned devices are checked and charged. The trial notes will continue to include equipment costs, charging problems, and comments about particular tracks.

on 14 March at Alder Mill's dye room, the log has batch 24-031, an 18 kilogram cotton run for slate blue, at vat C2. the schedule had it down for a 7:10 start, but the dyeing did not start until 7:46. Leon Park was the operator on the morning shift, and Nia Soto was the maintenance technician assigned to the room. The delay was not because the shade recipe had been changed or because the cotton was missing. The rinse return valve strainer was packed with lint, so the return flow was too low for the rinse cycle to begin. That was the practical cause of the late start, and the log records it after the inspection rather than as an explanation guessed beforehand.

At 7:18, Leon noticed the flow indicator holding below its usual mark and stopped the preparation step. He did not put dye into the vat while the return line was restricted. Nia checked the line and opened the strainer housing; she found lint pressed against the screen. In her note she wrote, “The return is barely moving; the strainer is full of lint.” She removed the lint, rinsed the screen, and put the housing back in place. The indicator rose after she restored the flow, and Leon recorded that the rinse cycle could proceed. The maintenance note gives the cleaning as the reason the restriction was cleared; it does not describe a valve replacement or any change to the dye formula.

The batch record says Leon began the rinse at 7:46 and used the normal rinse sequence. It lists the same slate-blue recipe that had been prepared for the run before the delay, with no revised quantities entered. The cotton weighed 18 kilograms at the start, and the recorded vat was C2 throughout the operation. The log gives a rinse-water temperature of 31 degrees Celsius and a first dye addition at 8:12. Those times matter because the start time in the daily plan is not the same as the start time of the actual rinse. The form has separate boxes for planned start, actual start, and first dye addition, and Leon filled all three rather than putting the later time in the margin.

1. Morning entry and correction

The first copy of the daily sheet showed 7:10 in the actual-start box, although the handwritten batch notes beside it gave 7:46. Leon drew one line through 7:10, left the original number readable, and entered 7:46 beside it. He initialed that correction and wrote “strainer clean” in the reason field. He did not erase the planned time from the schedule column. Nia signed the maintenance entry at 7:34, after cleaning the screen and before Leon began the rinse. The two entries therefore put the inspection and cleaning before the recorded actual start, rather than making it look as though the maintenance work happened after the batch was already running. The paper copy stayed in the room until the afternoon review.

The rinse continued without another interruption, according to Leon's shift notes. At 8:12 he added the first dye portion, and at 8:26 he noted that the liquor had reached the logged circulation mark. The next entries list the second addition at 8:41 and the final hold beginning at 9:05. He wrote down each time as it happened, not as a single retrospective account at the end of the shift. The record does not say that the delayed start changed the shade, shortened the hold, or required extra dye. It says only that the batch followed the listed recipe and that the standard checks were entered at their usual points. I kept those statements separate from the cause of the delay when I copied the account into the weekly notebook.

I felt embarrassed when I saw how easily the planned time could be mistaken for the actual one on the first copy. I may have sounded impatient when I asked Leon why both times appeared on the page, but I cannot be certain how my voice came across. He showed me the correction and explained that the schedule time belonged in its own column. That answer helped me understand the form, though my reaction was still embarrassment rather than anger at Leon or Nia. Neither of them had entered a false time: the first figure had been written in the wrong box, then corrected with the original still visible. I noted my uncertainty about my tone separately from the log's factual explanation of the delay.

At the afternoon review, I compared the paper sheet with the room's shift notebook. The notebook also lists the low return flow, the lint at the strainer, and Nia's cleaning work, with the same times for the inspection and the start. It does not include a photograph of the screen, and no photograph was added to the paper file that day. The daily sheet was clipped behind the maintenance note, while the recipe card remained with the batch papers. This arrangement made it possible to read the operational record in sequence, but it did not make the planned start disappear; that time remained visible in the schedule column.

The final log entry records the vat as released from the room at 10:18, after the listed checks were complete. The page does not say that I approved the batch, and I did not add an approval mark when copying the times into the weekly notebook. I wrote the actual start as 7:46, retained 7:10 as the planned time, and noted that the strainer had been cleaned before the rinse began. The notebook's next line is a separate inventory entry for the afternoon shift, recording two unopened screen-cleaning brushes in the maintenance drawer. That inventory line is not part of batch 24-031's process record.

The access list for the shared studio is kept in a locked cabinet beside the front desk, with a digital copy on the studio manager’s computer. A blue mark beside a name means that person has an active door code; it does not indicate permission to use every room or piece of equipment. The list is reviewed at the start of each month, but changes can be requested at any time.

Mara Ellison manages the list and handles requests from members, visiting instructors, and project partners. She checks each request against the person’s membership or the message from the staff member hosting them. When someone is added, Mara records the date, the expected length of access, and the rooms they may use. A member who needs only the print room, for example, is not automatically given access to the recording booth. Requests to add or remove a name should be sent to Mara by email or left in the labeled tray at the front desk. Each request needs the person’s full name and the reason for the change. Mara confirms the details before editing the list, and the host remains responsible for telling their guest which doors and areas are available to them.

Older copies are kept in a folder for three months so that staff can check when a code was issued or removed if a question arises. Mara has the dates from the residency coordinator but is waiting for the host member to confirm which rooms will be used. Until that detail is settled, she has not added the visiting group to the current sheet. The coordinator has been told that the access requests can be processed once the room information is confirmed.

The recipe card was clipped to the left side of the rack, and its numbers matched the copy kept in the office binder. Mara measured four hundred grams of indigo paste and two hundred grams of reducing agent, then added both to the vat with the wooden paddle. She used the long paddle because the short one had a crack near its handle. The tap water ran cloudy for about ten seconds and then cleared, so she filled the marked pail to the line and poured it slowly. The log notes that the room fan was on low and the back window stayed shut while the mixture settled for twenty minutes.

At nine twelve, Jonah came in from the rinse room carrying the shade strip from Monday’s trial. He held it next to the sample card under the neutral lamp and said, “The blue is warmer than the sample we approved yesterday, but leave the second vat alone.” The first comparison was made before the strip had fully dried, so Mara waited while Jonah hung it on the cord by the sink. After another eight minutes, they checked again, and the difference looked smaller. “Uh-huh,” Mara said when Jonah asked whether she had written down the waiting time. She added the minutes beside the reading rather than on the back of the card.

The first skein went into the vat at nine forty-five and stayed submerged for six minutes. Mara turned it twice with the paddle and lifted it slowly so the liquid could drain back into the basin. The cloth looked almost black when wet and showed a green edge under the lamp. They hung it on the upper rail with a blank space between it and the older sample because the older sample had a faint rust stain near one corner. The wash water in the first bucket was pale blue, the second was nearly clear, and the third carried a few loose fibers from the raw edge.

Well, the second skein took the same six-minute dip, but Mara recorded a lower vat reading after checking the glass thermometer again. The figure was sixty-six degrees, and the room had cooled when the fan stopped by itself. She restarted it and told no one to add heat until the maintenance check was done. The switch plate had felt warm on Monday, and a small note about that was already pinned above the workbench. The recipe did not call for a temperature change, and she kept the original measure of paste and reducing agent for the next dip. The time and amount remained the same.

Section Two: Shade Checks
By eleven thirty, the first two skeins were dry enough to compare with the approved strip. Mara laid them on clean white paper and turned each one so the light fell across the twill in the same direction. The first was a shade lighter than the card at the folded edge, while the second matched the middle of the sample more closely. She wrote both observations without calling either one a pass. The foreman had asked for a record before lunch and had not asked for a decision. The card was returned to its sleeve, and the damp strips were moved to a separate rail.

Like the first pair, the next test pieces came from the same roll, but one had been cut near the selvedge and the other from the center. The selvedge piece took up color faster along one side and left a narrow pale line after rinsing. Mara noted the location and width in the margin, then checked the cloth ticket to confirm that the cut pieces came from lot twenty-four B. The ticket number matched the tag on the cart. She did not change the vat or add more paste. The remaining cloth was covered with a clean sheet and left on the cart until the afternoon operator arrived.

Actually, the scale reading for the unused reducing agent was different from the morning estimate because the first weigh had included the paper cup. Mara weighed the sealed container again and entered the net amount in the supply column. The difference was thirty grams, and she left the earlier figure visible with a note beside it so the next reader could see both readings. The container went back into the locked cabinet, and the cabinet key was returned to its hook. No material was taken from the reserve shelf. By six on Thursday morning, Mara Venn had opened the blue canvas stall at the east entrance of Bellmarket. The delivery van from North Quay Produce was due before the first commuter rush, and its crates were needed for the day’s display of greens and apples. Rain had stopped during the night, but the paving stones were still slick. Mara put a rubber mat beside the counter and moved the weighing scale away from the edge, where passing shoppers sometimes caught its cord with their bags.

The order sheet listed thirty-two bunches of chard, twenty-four heads of fennel, eighteen kilograms of Cox apples, and twelve jars of orchard honey. Mara had asked for the honey to arrive in its cardboard tray because the jars were easier to count that way. The driver, Ellis, had called at 5:42 to say the van was delayed by roadworks near the canal bridge. He gave an estimated arrival time of 6:20, though he could not say how long the queue would last. Mara used the extra minutes to arrange the chalkboard and set out paper bags.

At 6:27, Ellis backed into the loading bay with the hazard lights blinking. His delivery note showed the produce quantities and a separate line for the returnable crate deposit. Mara checked that line before signing. The deposit was £18, and it was not part of the £146.40 charge for the food and honey. Ellis confirmed that the amount due for the order itself was £146.40; the deposit would be credited when the empty crates were collected. Mara wrote both amounts in the stall ledger so the till record would not combine them.

They unloaded the van in three trips. The chard was packed in shallow green boxes, while the fennel had been secured with paper bands inside a deeper crate. One box of apples had a damp corner, but the fruit inside was firm and unmarked. Ellis set the honey tray on the counter rather than stacking it with the produce. Mara counted the jars twice and found all twelve in place. She then checked the apple weight on the stall scale, which read 18.2 kilograms, two hundred grams above the order. Ellis noted the difference on his copy of the delivery sheet.

Mara’s handwritten receiving notes were arranged as follows:

1. Chard: 32 bunches received; leaves fresh, with two outer leaves removed from one bunch.
2. Fennel: 24 heads received; three had short stems, but all were sound.
3. Apples: 18.2 kilograms received; the additional 0.2 kilograms were not added to the invoice.
4. Honey: 12 jars received in one tray; seals intact.

The last point mattered because the morning total was being checked against a market voucher that covered food purchases but not container deposits. Mara entered £146.40 under produce and pantry goods, then recorded the £18 deposit in the separate returnables column. The voucher balance showed £160, leaving £13.60 available for another eligible purchase. She did not include the deposit when calculating that balance. Ellis initialled the note beside the two amounts, and Mara kept the yellow copy with the week’s other supplier records.

“Can you put the empty crates on the north side when you’re finished?” Ellis asked. “The collection driver comes after lunch, and he needs a clear path to the drain.” Mara pointed out that the flower stall next door sometimes left buckets in that space. Ellis said he would tell the collection driver to wait by the awning if the route was blocked. They agreed that the crates could stay behind Mara’s counter until then, as long as the honey tray was not put on top of them.

A customer arrived while Ellis was securing the van door and asked whether the apples were local. Mara showed him the label, which named the orchard outside Linton but did not give a picking date. She explained that the farm delivered twice a week and that this batch had come in that morning. The customer bought a paper bag of apples and two bunches of chard. Mara weighed the apples separately from the delivery check, charged the displayed stall price, and gave him the small receipt from the till. The sale did not change the figures in the supplier ledger.

Before leaving, Ellis took a photograph of the signed delivery sheet for the depot records. Mara asked him to make sure the image showed the note about the extra apple weight and the separate deposit, because both details were easy to miss on the narrow form. He checked the picture on his phone, then sent it to the depot while standing beside the van. The loading bay was clear again by 6:51, and Mara brought the rubber mat back under the counter.

The rest of the morning brought steady foot traffic but no further delivery. Mara moved the fennel into a wooden crate, placed the honey on the upper shelf, and kept the chard misted beneath a damp cloth. At 12:35, she stacked the empty returnable crates behind the counter with their labels facing outward. The flower stall’s buckets were still beside the drain, so she left the north-side route open and wrote a note for the collection driver directing him to the awning. The market office posted the afternoon stall map at one o’clock; Mara checked it before setting out the remaining apples.
